extracted.intended_audience: academic economists, empirical researchers, and policymakers studying mortgage markets, shadow banking, and lender classification
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and variable definitions for classifying lenders (traditional bank vs shadow bank; fintech vs non-fintech), defining loan outcomes (default, prepayment), and regression/specification choices used in empirical analysis of mortgage data (HMDA, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac).

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional bank versus shadow bank
rubrics_metrics.description: A lender is a traditional bank if it is a depository institution; otherwise, the lender is a shadow bank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: whether a lender is deposit-taking largely determines its exposure to banking regulation, which is central to the paper's analysis. Classification is done manually in many cases; HMDA's primary regulator field is used as a first cut (see below). Examples and manual overrides are described (e.g., Merrimack Mortgage Company classified as shadow bank despite FDIC regulation because it did not have deposits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-way lender classification (Traditional / Non-Fintech Shadow / Fintech Shadow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lenders are classified into one of three mutually exclusive categories: (1) Traditional Banks, (2) Non-Fintech Shadow Banks, and (3) Fintech Shadow Banks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure summarized in two steps: Step 1 — determine if lender is a traditional bank or shadow bank (depository status). If traditional, classification ends. Step 2 — if shadow bank, determine whether it is fintech or non-fintech. Note: the authors do not classify traditional banks as 'fintech traditional banks' or 'non-fintech traditional banks.' Further details for step implementations appear in Appendix A.7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use HMDA primary regulator as first-cut for classification
rubrics_metrics.description: HMDA identifies the lender’s primary regulator, which provides a useful first-cut regarding depository versus non-depository institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mapping and practical rules: OCC, OTS, and NCUA-regulated lenders were classified as banks (100% bank in HMDA mapping). The Federal Reserve-regulated lenders were manually classified (62.92% Bank / 37.08% Shadow Bank in their summary). For FDIC-regulated lenders, exceptions exist (e.g., Merrimack classified as shadow bank despite FDIC). For HUD-regulated lenders, most were treated as shadow banks (0.30% Bank / 99.70% Shadow Bank). For CFPB-regulated loans, most were classified as banks but some (e.g., Suntrust Mortgage) were classified as shadow banks. The text documents these regulator-to-classification distributions and notes manual review where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fannie Mae / Freddie Mac seller identification rule for large sellers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac data identify by name sellers who have comprised at least 1% of sales to the GSE within a given quarter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On average 15–20 uniquely identified lenders per quarter; across the sample they identify 55 unique lenders comprising between 50% and 85% market share in a given quarter. These identified lenders are manually classified as traditional or shadow banks based on depository status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Default (loan-level outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Default is defined as the loan status becoming 60 days past due within two years of origination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in analyses of loan performance (e.g., Table 7 and Appendix probit regressions). Data source: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac performance data (2010–2013 in discussed analyses). All regressions include year fixed effects; regressions with controls include borrower and loan controls described elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Prepayment (loan-level outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepayment is defined as the loan being prepaid within two years of origination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used alongside default in loan-performance analyses. Prepayment is the event of interest in Panel B of Table 7 and in probit specifications. The relationship between interest rates and prepayment is discussed as having ambiguous sign ex-ante; analyses control for year fixed effects and other borrower/loan covariates in robustness specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression fixed effects and control specification convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Columns (1), (3), and (5) (in many tables) include quarter fixed effects and no other controls; Columns (2), (4), and (6) include quarter × ZIP fixed effects and borrower controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paired specification (simple fixed-effect specification vs. richer ZIP×quarter + controls) is used repeatedly across tables (mortgage rates, loan performance, subgroup comparisons) to show robustness. The paper also indicates which columns include borrower-and-loan controls, lender fixed effects, nonlinear controls (polynomials), etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard errors clustering and significance notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard errors are clustered at the zip-quarter level; t-statistics in parentheses; * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This convention is stated repeatedly for tables using HMDA and GSE data. Interest rates and many left-hand-side variables are reported in percent; t-stats are shown in parentheses beside coefficient estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: All regulatory variables standardized
rubrics_metrics.description: All regulatory variables are standardized, so coefficients can be interpreted as percent change in shadow bank share for a one standard deviation change in the regulatory measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example regulatory measures include Δ Capital ratio (2008–2015 lending-weighted change), % MSR (lending-weighted 2008 fraction of MSR assets of tier-1 capital), Lawsuit exposure (lending-weighted exposure to mortgage-related lawsuits), and % OTS (share of mortgage originations regulated by the OTS in 2008). Standardization allows direct interpretation of coefficients as percent change per one SD shift; table notes report N, R2, and t-statistics; first-stage F-statistic for IV reported where applicable (48.68 in an example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental-variable strategy using capital ratio changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 2006–2008 capital ratio changes to instrument for 2008–2015 capital ratio changes in county-level regressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel B of Table 8 provides first-stage, reduced-form, and second-stage results: Column (1) is the first stage; Columns (2) and (4) are reduced form regressions; Columns (3) and (5) are the second stage regressions. The instrument's F-statistic is reported (48.68). County controls are included; regression is at the county level with sample size and R2 reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: High FICO dummy definition
rubrics_metrics.description: High FICO is a dummy variable for borrowers with FICO in the top decile for the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in interactions (High FICO × Fintech) to test heterogeneous pricing/effects (Table 10). Columns show full sample and sub-period analyses (2010–2013, 2014–2015) with quarter or quarter-zip fixed effects as noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conforming mortgage definition (HMDA / GSE linkage)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mortgage is conforming if it is conventional and reported as sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac in HMDA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: if the mortgage is sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac more than a year after origination it is not reported as sold in HMDA and hence not counted in the 'conforming' panel. Figures and tables that split by conforming loans use this definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical range for closing / origination fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Closing costs are typically 1–5% of the mortgage balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appendix provides anecdotal evidence that fintech lenders do not appear to offer lower origination fees and may be on the high end (example: Quicken Loans estimator gives 5.4% for a sample purchase; Bankrate reports a much lower average for Illinois). External sources and consumer-review anecdotes are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bootstrap procedure for R2 distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Each bootstrapped sample selects a random sample of originations with replacement, reruns the interest-rate regression, and records the R2s; bootstrap is run on 100 random samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show the distribution of bootstrapped R2s corresponding to different specifications of interest-rate determinants (e.g., FICO/LTV/quarter FE; all linear observables; all observables with up to third-degree terms). Panels A–C in Fig. 7 illustrate these bootstrap distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing significance of R2 differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests of significance of R2 differences follow Erickson and Whited (2002).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in Table 9 where R2 of different specifications explaining interest rates are compared across full sample, shadow bank sample, and subsamples (non-fintech vs fintech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probit specifications for relationship between interest rate and performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability that a loan defaults or prepays is modeled using probit regressions where the interest rate is an explanatory variable (equations 37–39), including versions with and without controls and interactions Rate × Fintech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel A reports default probit results; Panel B reports prepayment probit results. All regressions include year fixed effects; specifications with controls include borrower-and-loan controls. The appendix discusses interpretation (e.g., fintech rates appear slightly less related to default; fintech rates more strongly associated with prepayment) and caveats (investor awareness, selection into fintech). Pseudo-R2s and coefficient magnitudes are reported.
